introduction_markdown: Answer BOTH sections in the SAME answer booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity, (e.g your name, school, parentage etc) will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the Directed Writing question avoid indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer because this will earn you no marks. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Time allowed: two hours.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A - DIRECTED WRITING (30 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content (14 marks); Expression and Accuracy (12 marks); Slanting (04 marks).

You are a health worker and you are concerned with the people of your community who do not bother about the spread of diseases. Selecting relevant ideas from the passage below, write an article for a local newspaper on the factors responsible for the spread of diseases and possible methods of prevention.

Your article should be written in TWO paragraphs of not more than **150 words**. Write in a convincing manner, paying attention to grammar, spelling and handwriting.

**Passage**

Every day the body wages war against enemies that are silent and unseen but potentially deadly. Foreign invaders, such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites threaten our health. We may not be aware of those battles because our immune systems repel or destroy most of the invaders before the onset of symptoms.

For thousands of years, people knew virtually nothing about the dangers of microscopic or other small harmful organisms. However, when 19th century scientists confirmed the link between germs and disease, we became better equipped to defend ourselves. Medical researchers have since eliminated or greatly reduced the threat of infectious diseases, including smallpox and polio. Recently, however, others such as yellow fever, dengue, ebola, and corona are the topics of the time. There are factors responsible for the spread of these diseases. Every year, millions of people travel around the globe often transporting disease-causing agents. This is spread by international travellers. Some bacteria have developed resistance to antibiotics. "The world is heading towards post-antibiotic era in which common infections can once again kill," states the World Health Organization. Some germs can invade our bodies by riding on tiny droplets in someone's cough or sneeze. They can also spread through skin contact with body fluids from other people including blood and products derived from blood, so avoid hugging and shaking of hands. Do not underestimate the benefits of washing your hands thoroughly and frequently. It is perhaps the most effective way you can stop the spread of infections. Another cause is civil unrest and poverty. These often hinder government efforts to control the spread of diseases.

The best defence is to protect our water supply from contamination. If we know that the water supply is contaminated or suspect that it is, we should treat the water at home to make it safe. Also live in a community that properly disposes of human waste so that it does not contaminate local water supply. Contaminated fruits may look fresh and nutritious. So get into the habit of washing all fruits and vegetables. Some food require cooking at a certain temperature in order to destroy dangerous microbes. Avoid preparing food for others when you are sick. The fact that many people lack practical knowledge of how to prevent disease causes its spread. Limit contact with disease-carrying insects by staying indoors when they are active or wear protective clothing. Wash your hands after touching a domestic animal.

We live in a world plagued with potentially dangerous diseases. Take to heart these words of an ancient proverb: The shrewd one sees the danger and conceals himself.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (two paragraphs, 127 words)**

Dear readers, diseases spread silently, and too many of us ignore the danger. Germs travel with international travellers, some bacteria now resist antibiotics, and others ride on droplets from a cough or sneeze or pass through contact with body fluids, so avoid hugging and shaking hands. Poverty and civil unrest also hinder government efforts.

However, we can protect ourselves. Wash your hands thoroughly and frequently, which is perhaps the best defence. Treat suspect water at home and dispose of waste properly so that it never contaminates our water supply. Wash fruits and vegetables, cook food well, and do not prepare food for others when you are sick. Stay indoors when insects are active or wear protective clothing. Let us act today, for prevention is better than cure.

**Why this works (selection and slanting).** The article has a clear double purpose, the FACTORS that spread diseases and the METHODS of prevention, so the first paragraph keeps only causes (international travel, antibiotic resistance, droplets from coughs and sneezes, contact with body fluids and hugging or shaking hands, poverty and civil unrest) and the second keeps only protective actions (hand washing, treating suspect water, proper disposal of waste, washing fruits and vegetables, cooking food, not preparing food for others when sick, staying indoors or wearing protective clothing when insects are active). It leaves out everything that does not serve this purpose: the war-against-invaders image, the history of the 19th century scientists, the eradication of smallpox and polio, the list of recent diseases, the WHO quotation and the closing proverb. The tone is direct and convincing (address to the readers, imperatives, a call to action), the sentences are rephrased in the candidate's own words, and the answer is in exactly TWO paragraphs under 150 words.

**Marking guide**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content | 14 | Relevant points chosen from the passage: several factors in paragraph 1 and several methods of prevention in paragraph 2; no irrelevant history or background |
| Expression and Accuracy | 12 | Own words (no lifting of whole sentences), varied linking, correct grammar, spelling and punctuation, TWO paragraphs, 150 words at most |
| Slanting | 4 | The text is an article for a local newspaper that convinces readers of the danger and urges them to act (health worker's point of view) |

**Common mistakes**

1. Copying whole sentences from the passage: the instructions say indiscriminate copying earns no marks.
2. Mixing factors and prevention in one block, or writing only about causes or only about prevention, so that one half of the question is not answered.
3. Writing one paragraph or three or more paragraphs instead of TWO, or going over 150 words.
